title: 1.1 Using "h" and "p" elements for headings and paragraphs

levels.description: In web development, headings and paragraphs are the foundational elements that form the structure of content. HTML provides six heading tags, ranging from h1 to h6, which are used to define headings at different levels. h1 is the highest-level heading, typically used for the main title of a page, with the largest font and heaviest weight; h6 is the lowest-level heading, used for the most minor heading content. These headings not only affect visual presentation but are also crucial for the semantic structure of web pages and search engine optimization (SEO). Paragraphs are represented using the p tag, which wraps an independent block of text content. Browsers automatically add some space before and after a paragraph to distinguish it from other content. For example, you can use h1 for an article title and then use a p tag to write an introductory paragraph. These tags are all 'block-level elements' in HTML, meaning they occupy the entire width by default, starting on a new line and ending before the next line. Correct use of these tags helps build a clear, readable, and search-engine-friendly web page structure, which is a fundamental skill every front-end learner must master.

In practical web design, the combination of headings and paragraphs is very common. Typically, we use h1 for the main title of the page, such as the title of an article, then use h2 or h3 for subheadings of various sections, with one or more p elements following each subheading to display specific content. This structure not only makes it easier for readers to understand the hierarchy of the content but also helps assistive technologies like screen readers parse the page better. For example, on a news page, h1 might be the news headline, h2 could be the author and publication time, followed by several p tags describing the event, background information, and subsequent impact. Additionally, headings should maintain a logical progression, avoiding skipping levels; for instance, you should not use h4 directly after h1 but should follow the order of h2, h3 for gradual subdivision. The p tag can also be combined with other inline elements like strong or em to emphasize keywords and enhance expression. By reasonably matching these tags, you can create web content with a clear structure and explicit semantics, laying a good foundation for subsequent style design and interactive development.

To deeply understand the h series tags and p tag, one must start with HTML semantics and the Document Outline mechanism. HTML5 introduced more intelligent structural rules; browsers and search engines automatically build the page's structure tree based on the hierarchy of headings. Although most browsers currently show obvious visual style differences for h1 to h6, from a semantic perspective, they collectively constitute the hierarchical structure of the page. Modern development recommends using only one h1 per page to represent the page theme, with the remaining headings used logically nested from h2 to h6. Furthermore, structural elements like section and article can reset the heading hierarchy, allowing h1 to be reused in different blocks without disrupting the overall structure. Although the p tag is simple, its 'paragraph' semantics cannot be replaced by div, because div is a non-semantic container, while p explicitly represents a block of text. Misusing div instead of p leads to loss of semantics, affecting accessibility and SEO. At the same time, browsers have default margins for p tags, which developers often reset via CSS for more precise layout control. Mastering these underlying mechanisms helps in writing more professional and standard-compliant HTML code.

To consolidate the understanding of heading and paragraph tags, let's complete a comprehensive exercise: create a webpage fragment about 'Front-end Learning Guide'. First, use an h1 tag to write the main title 'Front-end Development Beginner's Guide', which will be the core theme of the entire page. Then, add an h2 tag below it with the content 'What is Front-end Development', followed by a p tag with the text 'Front-end development refers to building the parts of a webpage that users can directly see and interact with, mainly involving three technologies: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.' Next, add another h2 title 'Learning Path Suggestions', and use two p tags to write 'Step 1: Master HTML structure and syntax; Step 2: Learn CSS styling and layout.' Ensure all elements are arranged in order to form a clear reading flow. You can use the browser's developer tools to check the element structure and confirm that the heading hierarchy is reasonable. This exercise simulates the structure of a real document, helping you understand how to organize content with h and p tags. Note: do not use line breaks within a p tag to create paragraphs; each natural paragraph should be wrapped in an independent p tag, which is the correct semantic practice.
